data.title: Stop sibling result polling when an async group fails
data.body:
When one result in `aget_result_group()` raises, `asyncio.gather()` leaves the other result pollers running. A missing result can then be polled indefinitely after the caller has already received the error.

Keep references to the result-wait tasks and cancel and await any unfinished ones before returning or propagating an exception. This stops only local result polling; queued Huey tasks are not revoked. Tests cover failure cleanup, continued execution of the queued task, caller cancellation, and existing successful group results.

Validation:
- The failure-cleanup regression fails on unchanged `dbd1aef`; the other five asyncio tests pass there.
- Python 3.13.14: 135 asyncio/API/wrapper/immediate-mode tests pass. Python 3.10.20: all six asyncio helper tests pass.
- `git diff --check` passes. The full backend/consumer test suite was not run.

data.body: **Backwards-incompatible.** The django stats app writes to its own sqlite database by default (`huey-stats.db` in `settings.BASE_DIR`), instead of `DATABASES['default']`. To keep recording in your main Django database, specify the database explicitly: ```python HUEY_STATS = {'database': 'postgresql://user:password@localhost/my_db'} ``` `HUEY_STATS['database']` takes a db-url or a peewee `Database`, or use `HUEY_STATS['filename']` to set the sqlite path. See the Django docs section for building a peewee database from your existing `DATABASES` entry. The admin *Events* log is now rendered from the stats database through peewee, rather than being a `ModelAdmin` via ORM. It is now linked from the dashboard's *Recent events* heading. --- Consumer: * Add `--shutdown-timeout` option to bound graceful shutdown time. * Add `--graceful-signal` option to allow making SIGTERM the graceful shutdown signal (e.g. ``-g TERM``). User-facing APIs: * Add `ttl` to `lock_task()` and `put_if_empty()` so locks expire on their own. Supported by memory and redis storages, others raise `NotImplementedError`. `RedisHuey` requires server hash-field TTL support (redis 7.4+ or valkey 9+), `RedisExpireHuey` works on any version. * Add `timeout` parameter to `aget_result()`. Small stuff: * Ensure one raising signal receiver does not prevent the remaining receivers from running. * Fix crontab ranges with a step (`0-30/5`) and wrap-around ranges (`22-2`, `day_of_week='1-7'`). Raise `ValueError` when a field matches no values. * Pass failed chord members to the callback as `huey.Error` and skipped (revoked, expired, cancelled) members as `huey.SKIPPED` instead of a raw exception or `None`. * Delete chord partial results explicitly on completion, so they no longer linger until expiry on `RedisExpireStorage`. * Write the error of a failed pipeline stage to every skipped downstream stage, so their `Result` handles raise instead of blocking. * Accept an explicit `id` in `TaskWrapper.s()`, matching `schedule()`. Storage: * Skip messages that fail to deserialize in `Huey.pending()` and `Huey.scheduled()`, logging the error, as `read_schedule()` already does. * Add `clean_name` option to `RedisHuey` (default to `True`). Specify `False` to stop stripping non-alphanumeric characters from the storage namespace. The default will change in a future release. * Reduce Redis round-trips for `peek_data`, `pop_data` and `delete_data`, and make `RedisExpireStorage.incr()` set the TTL atomically w/ the increment. * Skip the exclusive lock in `SqliteStorage.dequeue()` when the queue is empty, so idle consumers no longer block producers and the scheduler. * Batch the `SqliteStorage.read_schedule()` delete to avoid sqlite's parameter limit when many tasks come due at once. Same fix in `SqlHuey`. * Order `SqliteStorage.read_schedule()` and `SqlHuey.read_schedule()` by `(timestamp, id)`, matching `PostgresStorage`. * Add `queue` to the sqlite task index (`task_queue_priority_id`) so queues sharing a file no longer scan each other's rows. The old `task_priority_id` index is dropped when the schema is initialized. I'll get rid of the temporary in-band drop in a few releases. * Add `peek_many()` to the storage API. Revocation checks now fetch the task and task-class keys in one round trip. * Return str keys from `result_items()` on every storage backend. Redis and File storage previously returned bytes. Stats: * Better handling for `timeout`, `locked`, `rate-limited` and `retrying` in stats recorder. * Log dropped events in the stats recorder instead of failing silently. * Fix stats recorder `max_events` pruning to count rows per queue. With multiple queues sharing a stats db, each queue retained only a fraction of the configured cap. * Add `inflight_hours` option to stats recorder, replacing the hardcoded 6 hour in-flight cutoff. * Require the `change_hueydashboard` permission for the django admin dashboard's revoke, restore and flush controls. data.title: When are tasks acknowledged?
data.body:
When are Huey tasks acknowledged? In comparison with Celery, it has a `task_acks_late` to only acknowledge a task after it has been executed.

Sorry if this covered by the docs, I couldn't find anything.

Huey doesn't use an amqp-style workflow, nor does it attempt to ensure at-least-once delivery. There's no ack. The workflow, once a worker begins a task, is simple:

* Execute task
* If unhandled exception occurs and the task has one or more retries, it is re-enqueued.
* If the task finishes successfully, the return value is placed in the result store (though None return values are not stored by default).

data.title: Automatically consume an unfinished task if the Huey consumer is restarted
data.body:
Our Huey consumer restarts sometimes (it can be planned or unplanned maintenance, version upgrade, etc.).

Whenever this happens, tasks that are in the middle of consumption are "lost" and won't be retied.

Is it possible to add a mark in the Redis queue only after a task was completed (either successfully or unsuccessfully) so that if Huey is restarted the same task is picked up once more?

Huey is not guaranteed at-least-once delivery, and does not do acknowledgement of completed tasks. The consumer supports a soft shutdown for this reason -- any in-flight tasks will be finished before the consumer exits. It sounds like you are not using this, however.

You can add a signal handler for the `SIGNAL_INTERRUPTED` signal, which is run when a task is interrupted during execution (by a hard shutdown) - using this signal you can add logic to handle tasks that are interrupted during execution:

https://huey.readthedocs.io/en/latest/signals.html

@coleifer I found this discussion and your recommendation useful and worth adding to documentation, some minimal example would be awesome. I believe it's quite common to restart workers on deployment to reload tasks code, and sometimes tasks are just too long, i.e. video processing etc.

3e7bdf253a02813eff138a2db6b00554d81a8e57 - hopefully this helps clarify.

Docs here: https://huey.readthedocs.io/en/latest/consumer.html#consumer-shutdown

data.title: Retry Tasks on SIGTERM?
data.body:
Saw the following in the docs and having a bit of trouble interpreting it:
> Warning Huey does not guarantee at-least-once delivery of messages, and does not do acknowledgement of completed tasks. This means that if you terminate the consumer without letting it finish any currently-executing tasks, those tasks will be lost. To be alerted when this occurs, you can use Huey’s [Signals](https://huey.readthedocs.io/en/latest/signals.html#signals) (specifically signals.SIGNAL_INTERRUPTED). The consumer will emit this for tasks that are interrupted during execution.

Let's say I send a SIGTERM signal to a consumer, and I have multiple consumers running (in a distributed fashion). Is there a way I can ensure this task will be added back to the queue and retried by another consumer?

data.title: is this to replace Celery
data.body: that was just a discussion opener. :) I am back to follow all of Charles projects and add them to my toolkit.

When I wrote huey, which was some time ago, it was partly in response to what I perceived to be the extreme complexity of `celery`. Before 3.0, celery had lots of dependencies and required lots of configuration.

Huey differs from celery in that:
- Less dependencies
- Less configuration
- Threaded model as opposed to multi-process
- Less features

I designed huey for people who need a task queue for simple things like:
- sending emails
- generating thumbnails
- making API calls
- checking spam

If you have any of the following needs, then celery is probably a better choice for you:
- ~~CPU-bound tasks.~~ (huey has process-based workers now)
- Distribute tasks to multiple processes, possibly on multiple hosts.
- Dedicate particular workers to particular tasks.
- Sophisticated workflows.
- Auto-scaling and built-in rate-limiting.

> * Distribute tasks to multiple processes, possibly on multiple hosts.
> * Dedicate particular workers to particular tasks.
> * Sophisticated workflows.
> * Auto-scaling and built-in rate-limiting.

Wondering what you would write here 10 years later? @coleifer

I'd write celery, more like smellery.

Seriously though I don't know what all has changed in celery over the years (or the other popular projects in this space). huey's gotten better at a few things since I wrote that, though, so I can write about that. Over the years, Huey's added:

* different worker types, so it can handle a variety of workloads
* priorities
* locking
* pipelines/chaining tasks
* signalling / much more powerful hooks for extending and introspecting huey
* controllable shutdown behavior - graceful or hard
* additional storage backends for different types of deployments

Things huey is not great for:

* at-least-once tasks (we are at-most-once as it is simpler)
* complex pipelines / airflow-type stuff
* monitoring tooling / etc is not on the level of celery ecosystem

huey still remains stupid simple to get going with and can go rather far. I think the users who like huey like it quite well, and that's what I'm going for here.
Personally been using it for probably about 7 years and in all honesty a big fan!

data.title: About greenlet worker and OS signals
data.body:
Hi! I'm using the `Greenlet` worker, and noticed that if a signal is received while one of the greenlets is executing (i.e. not "blocked" waiting for I/O), it will be that "thread" the one who handles the signal.

This leads to a somehow troublesome behavior. For instance, when a `SIGINT` is received, it can lead to only one greenlet being stopped, instead of the whole event loop (the other greenlets keep going on).

I just wanted to know your thoughts on this. Is there a way to force that the signal is handled outside the event loop? Should I even worry about this, as the chances of it happening should be extremely low (tasks are heavy on I/O, not CPU)?
Let me investigate, thanks for the report.

I've added a change in 361e380 that seems to address the issue you described, as well as a potential separate issue where a SIGTERM is handled, but does not actually interrupt the running (blocking) task.

Do you mind pulling those changes in and taking a look when you have time?

Thanks for the quick reply! I did some experiments, and I think that those changes solve the problem. In any case, I leave here my findings as it may be helpful to you:

## 1. SIGTERM:
### 1.1. When no greenlet is executing, the signal is handled by the main thread.
In this case, the signal handler will raise a `KeyboardInterrupt`, which is captured and handled as a `SIGINT` by the consumer (i.e. graceful shutdown).

If there are greenlets "waiting" for an I/O result, the consumer will wait on them (via `.join`) instead of interrupting them. Otherwise the consumer will just exit.

### 1.2. When there is a greenlet executing, the signal is handled by the greenlet.

In this case, the signal handler stops the execution of the running greenlet, and sets the necessary flags for the consumer to shutdown (not gracefully).

If there were no other greenlets ready to be run, the consumer will exit right away.

If a greenlet was waiting for the result of an I/O operation, the consumer will also exit right away and that particular result will be lost (which is expected). Nonetheless, Huey's `SIGNAL_INTERRUPTED` will be triggered.

If there were other greenlets waiting to be run, one of them will start executing (despite the consumer already exiting). This will not block the main thread, but the task being run will be lost (no `SIGNAL_INTERRUPTED` will be triggered).

In my case, I'm reenqueuing a task in a `SIGNAL_INTERRUPTED` hook. This leads to the reenqueued task to starts executing in one of the greenlets, and then being lost (which I know is not Huey's problem as it doesn't try to achieve at-least-once execution).

## 2. SIGINT:
### 2.1. When no greenlet is executing, the signal is handled by the main thread.
This case is the same as `1.1.`, because it will trigger a graceful shutdown.

### 2.2. When there is a greenlet executing, the signal is handled by the greenlet.
In this case, the greenlet will continue executing (it will not be stopped by the signal). Once it finishes, one of two things can happen depending on whether there is a greenlet ready for execution up next. If that is the case, it will start executing. Otherwise, the consumer will enter graceful shutdown mode, and it will wait for all the greenlets to finish.
I may need to get a little more clever with this - let me think on it some more and see if I can't get the behavior to more precisely match the threads/processes.
Awesome! Let me know if I can help with anything.

I'm not quite sure yet what the best option will be, but [this](https://github.com/gevent/gevent/issues/799) clarifies a bit some of the difficulty:

>Signal handlers run in the main thread and the main greenlet in that thread (whether anything is patched or not). The main greenlet is running the hub, and things that run in the hub can't switch out. Trying to join a greenlet-based thread requires switching.

Looking at the [source](https://www.gevent.org/_modules/gevent/signal.html) (and by testing locally), the signal handlers are all run on the gevent Hub. As the comment indicates, we can't switch there.

I've tried making a small change here:

9cbf17eb025dab84a2c7afcd702543a4fe82d88f

Testing locally it looks to be working OK.

The behavior I'm observing with the above change (9cbf17e) is:

* SIGINT
  * no tasks: exits cleanly
  * io-bound tasks: waits til they finish, exits cleanly
  * mix of io-bound and cpu-bound tasks: waits til they finish, exits cleanly
* SIGTERM
  * no tasks, exits cleanly
  * io-bound tasks: exits immediately, interrupted task signal fires
  * mix of io-bound and cpu-bound tasks: waits til the cpu-bound tasks finish(!), notifies any interrupted tasks, exits cleanly

I'm not sure we can do a whole lot better than that, but am open to ideas. Closing for now.

I don't see this. In the `examples/simple` directory in this repo there is a task that just sleeps for however long you specify. Here is output of interrupting that task while it is running when using 4 worker threads:

data.title: About SIGINT, SIGTERM and SIGKILL
data.body:
Hi, not really an issue, but rather a question/doubt about how these signals work in the context of Huey.

I've been reading the docs and other issues, and my current understanding is:
1. Outside of Huey:
  * SIGINT/SIGTERM are used to request a process termination, thus they are mechanisms through which one can implement a graceful shutdown.
  * SIGKILL on the other hand, terminates it on the spot, leaving no space for cleanup.
2. Within Huey:
  * SIGINT is used to request process termination, which allows for extra graceful shutdown (i.e. workers are allowed to finish the tasks they are working on, but no new tasks will be started).
  * SIGTERM is used to "force" the termination of the workers (i.e tasks that are currently executing will end abruptly, and of course, no new tasks will be started). I say "force" (between quotes) because it's not as brute as the SIGKILL signal, because there is some sort of "graceful" shutdown. More concretely, you can execute some cleanup actions, like requeuing the task in order to retry it later. One would do this by adding a handler to the `SIGNAL_INTERRUPTED` Huey signal (do not confuse with OS signals).
  * SIGKILL is not handled by Huey (and can't be by definition of that signal). Usually one would expect a SIGKILL coming after a SIGTERM, therefore, whatever cleanup task you do within your `SIGNAL_INTERRUPTED` handler, you better make sure it's fast.

Note: I only mentioned what happens with the worker processes/threads, and left aside the main process and the scheduler process (which are also part of the Huey consumer), because for now I'm only concerned about the workers.

Having said that, my question is: is my understanding correct? Particularly around using a `SIGNAL_INTERRUPTED` handler to requeue a task that was abruptly ended.

Note: I'm concerned about what would happend in the context of a deployment, where the cloud provider I use sends first a SIGTERM and then a SIGKILL (30 seconds later). I don't mind that the running tasks aren't able to finish in that same execution, so I don't really need to capture the SIGTERM sent by the OS, and transform it into a SIGINT before passing it down to Huey. For me, ending the tasks abruptly, but requeuing them for a later retry is enough.

Let me know what you think, and thanks for building such a great product!

Huey:

* SIGINT (e.g. Ctrl+C) performs graceful shutdown. Any currently-executing tasks will finish before the consumer stops.
* SIGTERM will shutdown immediately and send the huey `SIGNAL_INTERRUPTED` for any tasks that were interrupted.
* SIGKILL immediately kills the process.

SIGKILL may be sent by a process manager if the process does not exit quickly enough after receiving a SIGTERM - depends on how you have it configured.

>Having said that, my question is: is my understanding correct? Particularly around using a SIGNAL_INTERRUPTED handler to requeue a task that was abruptly ended.

Yes, that's pretty much the main use-case for the huey signal SIGNAL_INTERRUPTED.

It's probably ideal to have your process manager instead send a `SIGINT` if you want to avoid losing tasks that are running, but with 30s you should have tons of time to re-enqueue any tasks that are interrupted after a `SIGTERM` is sent.

> Yes, that's pretty much the main use-case for the huey signal SIGNAL_INTERRUPTED.

Awesome! And thank you very much for the quick reply.

> It's probably ideal to have your process manager instead send a SIGINT if you want to avoid losing tasks that are running, but with 30s you should have tons of time to re-enqueue any tasks that are interrupted after a SIGTERM is sent.

In my case, these are long running tasks (~5 minutes each). So, even if I changed the `SIGTERM` signal sent by the OS to a `SIGINT`, the task may not have enough time to finish before the OS sends the deadly `SIGKILL`.

Additionally, its worth mentioning that I have no control over those 30 seconds I mentioned previously, as that timeout is managed by the cloud provider. This means that increasing that timeout to a certain value where any task can finish within it, is not feasible for me.

Anyhow, thanks again for your response!

Hi @coleifer, sorry for bringing this up again, but I have additional questions that I'd hope you could help me with.

I looked into the code and realized what you meant when you said that the scheduler thread and the worker thread were "shutdown immediately" upon receiving a SIGTERM, and that "to avoid losing tasks that are running" I should change the SIGTERM signal for a SIGINT signal.

My main issue with changing the SIGTERM for a SIGINT, is that workers that are running a task will not be stopped. As I mentioned before, my tasks are long running tasks that take ~5 minutes to execute.

Having said that, is there an alternative that mixes both approaches? More concretely, one that doesn't "shutdown immediately" the threads, allowing them to perform cleaning actions such as those added through the `on_shutdown` hook, but also abruptly stops the execution of the tasks (and emits the corresponding `SIGNAL_INTERRUPTED` for each task).

What do you think about that behavior? 

------------------------------------------
Notes for other people that may read this:
- The "immediate shut down" of the scheduler thread can occur after the thread has removed tasks from the schedule, but before it has enqueued them. Therefore, you may lose these scheduled tasks.
- The "immediate shut down" of the worker threads can occur after the thread has dequeued a task, but before it has added it to the `huey._tasks_in_flight` set. Therefore, you will not receive a `SIGNAL_INTERRUPTED` for these tasks.

This behavior is consistent with the fact that Huey is an "at most once" queue, not an "at least once" queue ([relevant issue](https://github.com/coleifer/huey/issues/733#issuecomment-1525932810)).

The `on_shutdown` hooks are called by the worker processes themselves and are intended for clean-up actions within the worker during a graceful shutdown, [see doc](https://huey.readthedocs.io/en/latest/api.html#Huey.on_shutdown). An example might be a connection pool within the context of the worker process, to be used by tasks executed on that worker. These hooks are not called or used when a shutdown via `SIGTERM` is requested.

If you wish to re-enqueue a task that is interrupted due to a `SIGTERM` / immediate-shutdown, it should be done with the huey `SIGNAL_INTERRUPTED`. Yes there is a possibility that a task could be lost in the brief window between schedule -> queue or queue -> in flight (executing), and yes this is a consequence of the at-most-once design.

This is why I recommend that people use the graceful shutdown.

I don't believe there's much to suggest other than:

1. Use huey's `SIGNAL_INTERRUPTED` to re-enqueue interrupted tasks
2. Break your tasks into smaller pieces.
3. Add pre-execute and post-execute handlers to write / remove tasks from a secondary storage like the DB and audit the "gap" during restarts (e.g. tasks that were started but not finished/removed).
4. Wrap your consumer with a parent/wrapper script that traps `SIGTERM` and, when it is received, send the wrapped consumer a SIGINT and allows up to (say) 25s for it to terminate before sending a SIGTERM.
5. Add your own storage engine/layer that provides better guarantees.
6. Switch to an at-least-once tool.

Are these 5 minute tasks triggered by an external event of some kind, or do they run on a predictable schedule? You may be better off using a different tool if the latter.

> Are these 5 minute tasks triggered by an external event of some kind, or do they run on a predictable schedule?
The former, basically an HTTP request from a UI.

And, thanks for your input! I was actually thinking of a very similar approach to what you suggest. It's always nice to have some sort of validation that what one is thinking makes sense to others, so I really appreciate it.

-----------------------------------------
Summary of the suggested approach (in case someone else reads this):
1. Wrap consumer with a parent script that traps `SIGTERM`, sends the consumer a `SIGINT` and waits `X` seconds for it to terminate before sending a `SIGTERM`. `X` should leave enough time for the consumer to shutdown after it receives the `SIGTERM`, considering that in 30s the container will receive a `SIGKILL` (from the cloud provider). That's why `@coleifer` used 25s as an example, which would leave 5s to the consumer to shutdown after the `SIGTERM`.
2. If all tasks were able to finish within the interval defined by `X`, then we are all good. Otherwise some tasks will be terminated abruptly. In order to avoid losing those jobs, it's necessary to setup a handler for Huey `SIGNAL_INTERRUPTED`. This signal will be called for every task that gets interrupted, and inside the handler we should re-schedule/re-enqueue the task.
3. When the Huey consumer is forced to stopped (vía SIGTERM), it will not perform shutdown hooks. This will happen when a running task didn't finish within the interval defined by `X`. This means that, if you are using shutdown hooks to perform cleaning operations, such as closing db connections, these connections will be left unclosed (on the db server side). One way to handle this is to have the db server reap inactive connections after some time.
4. Note that by giving some time to the Huey consumer to shutdown gracefully, we are eliminating the risk of it shutting down during critical windows such as the mentioned before (i.e. scheduler pops tasks, but didn't have time to enqueue them, or worker dequeues tasks but didn't have time to add it to the `_tasks_in_flight` set). Therefore, there shouldn't be any lost of tasks due to the reasons aforementioned.

Having said that, Huey implements an "at most once" approach, so it's always possible that something out of what's controllable fails, and that tasks are lost.

-----------------------------------------

EDIT: The second signal sent should be another `SIGINT`, and not a `SIGTERM`. Otherwise, the consumer will stay hanged waiting for the worker thread that's executing the long task to finish, instead of continuing its own execution (in which it sends the `SIGNAL_INTERRUPTED`). cc: @coleifer

@abannura one way to handle this is to alter the behaviour of `_handle_stop_signal` and `stop` to stop gracefully with a timeout on a `SIGTERM`.
See the snippet below for an example.
Note that you'd still need a `SIGNAL_INTERRUPTED` handler for re-queuing tasks that don't complete.

```python
class GracefulTerminationConsumer(Consumer):
    def __init__(self, *args: Any, **kwargs: Any):
        super().__init__(*args, **kwargs)
        self._graceful_timeout = None

    def _handle_stop_signal(
        self,
        sig_num: Any,
        frame: Any,
    ):
        """
        Handles SIGTERM gracefully.
        The consumer blocks until the workers finish executing their tasks,
        for at most `SIG_TERM_TIMEOUT` seconds.
        If the workers are not finished, the workers are forcefully stopped.
        """
        self._graceful_timeout = SIG_TERM_TIMEOUT
        super()._handle_stop_signal(sig_num, frame)

    def stop(self, graceful: bool = False):
        if self._graceful_timeout is None:
            super().stop(graceful)
        else:
            self._stop_gracefully_with_timeout(self._graceful_timeout)

    def _stop_gracefully_with_timeout(self, timeout_delay: int):
        """
        Blocks the consumer while shutting down workers for at most `timeout_delay` seconds.
        """
        self.stop_flag.set()
        self._logger.info(
            f"Shutting down gracefully with {timeout_delay} second timeout..."
        )
        processes = [
            self.scheduler,
            *(worker_process for _, worker_process in self.worker_threads),
        ]

        # Non-blocking shut down of all processes.
        for process in processes:
            process.join(timeout=0)

        elapsed_seconds = 0
        start_time = time.monotonic()
        while elapsed_seconds < timeout_delay:
            if all(not self.environment.is_alive(p) for p in processes):
                # Exit loop if all processes have successfully shut down.
                self._logger.info("All workers have stopped gracefully.")
                break
            time.sleep(0.1)
            elapsed_seconds = time.monotonic() - start_time
        else:
            self._logger.info("Graceful termination timed out!")
```

@coleifer not sure how open you are to changing how `SIGTERM` is handled to something similar to this?

PS: If you're running your consumers as part of something like an autoscaling group, another thing that could help is tracking the running tasks on your instances and creating a custom termination policy to only terminate instances not running any tasks.

data.title: [OPEN] Tasks states are not maintained in case the worker is killed by the running task.
data.body:
As mentioned in the issue bellow, the tasks states are not maintained in case the worker is kill by the running task.  

https://github.com/coleifer/huey/issues/728#issuecomment-1521698502

In case we see an error log similar to the following, the currently running task is lost:

```log
20:27:54 Sleeping for 0.9978511869999238                                                  
20:27:54 Checking worker health.                                                          
20:27:54 Worker 2 died, restarting.                                                       
20:27:54 Scheduler is up and running.                                                     
``` 
The following code sections clearly shows this behavior:

https://github.com/coleifer/huey/blob/cc439d55890033a32443e79a2cd483979c2a672c/huey/consumer.py#L479

https://github.com/coleifer/huey/blob/cc439d55890033a32443e79a2cd483979c2a672c/huey/consumer.py#L455

It is also clear that the `dequeue` and `execute` methods do not record the worker `id` the execution is scheduled:

https://github.com/coleifer/huey/blob/cc439d55890033a32443e79a2cd483979c2a672c/huey/consumer.py#L110

https://github.com/coleifer/huey/blob/cc439d55890033a32443e79a2cd483979c2a672c/huey/consumer.py#L118

I do not expect this issue will be solved, but should at least emphasized in the documentation.

If the OOM killer is your issue, then you have bigger problems than huey. Simply retrying the task is unlikely to be of any help. At any rate, Huey is an at-most once task queue with explicit retries. An at-least-once task queue requires a concept of a visibility timeout (e.g. SQS/beanstalk) and an explicit ACK from the worker when the task is finished. We do not use this task queueing design out of a desire for simplicity. My opinion is that if you see OOM errors in your tasks, it is a sign that you need to buy more memory or redesign your tasks.

I have nothing to do with the code inside the task, I'm only responsible for the back-end and infrastructure to schedule those tasks and give for the end user a clear information about the task result. My end users are currently unhappy as they see `In Progress` task in the list.
Where are you pulling this "In Progress" from?
That is the last state _we maintain_ before we lose the task that is killed.  (updated)
Where is that state coming from?
How do you suggest to track `Completed` or `Failed` task?
You still have not answered my original question. Answer it or don't, it's up to you, but quit wasting my time.

I don’t intend to waste anyone’s time. That’s why I suggest we document this behavior of killed worker/task and emphasize it. As previously mentioned, the `In Progress` status is a derived one that we maintain in our backend service. It represents the state of tasks after the `SIGNAL_EXECUTING` signal. If the worker dies, no signal is sent related to the specific task that was running on the worker. Therefore, our backend cannot record any updates.

data.title: Configurable signal handler
data.body:
Hi @coleifer. Thanks for Huey.

We're evaluating Huey as a replacement for RQ and there is a lot to like here!

One hiccup is around how consumer signals are handled/interpreted. Since we're on Heroku, and Heroku [sends a SIGTERM](https://devcenter.heroku.com/articles/dynos#shutdown) right off the bat for a "graceful shutdown", means that the Huey consumer could be basically killed mid-action and thus lose work.

I don't think there is a way to configure what signals the Heroku dyno system sends — it looks like SIGTERM, followed by SIGKILL if the process hasn't shut down after 30 seconds — so we're wondering if there is scope in Huey to make signal handlers configurable?

I saw another issue outlining the same situation (#239) and there is a workaround in there, but the workaround feels like a hack.

Just wondering what your thoughts are on this. Cheers.

I'd suggest wrapping the consumer, then, in a small bash script which traps/handles the signals as you would like it to.

Huey uses sigterm to stop everything because it's a task queue and who knows how long a misbehaving task might stay running for? If TERM was for "graceful" shutdown, you'd need to use SIGKILL to force stop which means no cleanup on any number of worker/child processes. Just as a side note, if you need exactly once/at-least once you might want something more robust than redis / huey anyways.

Thanks for the answer.

> If TERM was for "graceful" shutdown, you'd need to use SIGKILL to force stop which means no cleanup on any number of worker/child processes.

Yeah.. I don't really understand why Heroku have done like that, probably because they want to have some guarantees that when they terminate a service, it really terminates, whether gracefully via TERM or "for sure" via KILL.

Wrapping is a good idea. Playing around with that now.

Another thing I realised is that if I have a task that's set to be retried N times and if the consumer is shut down or killed before the task has managed to successfully run, the task won't be retried when the consumer comes back up, even if it had retries left. Not sure if that's intended or not.

> if you need exactly once/at-least once you might want something more robust than redis / huey anyways

Yep, makes sense.

items.body:
I'm running the huey consumer on AWS ECS, and unfortunately it's not possible to configure the service to send `SIGINT` to request a container to stop. Instead, it always sends `SIGTERM` (and `SIGKILL` after a timeout).

While it would be preferable to tell ECS to send the right signal, it would be great to be able to tell the huey consumer to _also_ shutdown gracefully on `SIGTERM`.

items.title: About SIGINT, SIGTERM and SIGKILL
items.body:
Hi, not really an issue, but rather a question/doubt about how these signals work in the context of Huey.

I've been reading the docs and other issues, and my current understanding is:
1. Outside of Huey:
  * SIGINT/SIGTERM are used to request a process termination, thus they are mechanisms through which one can implement a graceful shutdown.
  * SIGKILL on the other hand, terminates it on the spot, leaving no space for cleanup.
2. Within Huey:
  * SIGINT is used to request process termination, which allows for extra graceful shutdown (i.e. workers are allowed to finish the tasks they are working on, but no new tasks will be started).
  * SIGTERM is used to "force" the termination of the workers (i.e tasks that are currently executing will end abruptly, and of course, no new tasks will be started). I say "force" (between quotes) because it's not as brute as the SIGKILL signal, because there is some sort of "graceful" shutdown. More concretely, you can execute some cleanup actions, like requeuing the task in order to retry it later. One would do this by adding a handler to the `SIGNAL_INTERRUPTED` Huey signal (do not confuse with OS signals).
  * SIGKILL is not handled by Huey (and can't be by definition of that signal). Usually one would expect a SIGKILL coming after a SIGTERM, therefore, whatever cleanup task you do within your `SIGNAL_INTERRUPTED` handler, you better make sure it's fast.

Note: I only mentioned what happens with the worker processes/threads, and left aside the main process and the scheduler process (which are also part of the Huey consumer), because for now I'm only concerned about the workers.

Having said that, my question is: is my understanding correct? Particularly around using a `SIGNAL_INTERRUPTED` handler to requeue a task that was abruptly ended.

Note: I'm concerned about what would happend in the context of a deployment, where the cloud provider I use sends first a SIGTERM and then a SIGKILL (30 seconds later). I don't mind that the running tasks aren't able to finish in that same execution, so I don't really need to capture the SIGTERM sent by the OS, and transform it into a SIGINT before passing it down to Huey. For me, ending the tasks abruptly, but requeuing them for a later retry is enough.

Let me know what you think, and thanks for building such a great product!

items.title: Killed consumer process not restarted
items.body:
If a process type worker is killed via SIGKILL (i.e. from Linux OOM killer) the call to `proc.is_alive()` in the health check still returns true and the process is never restarted. Note that currently the process is left as a zombie process, but even if SIGCHLD is ignored by the parent, the process would no longer exist but `proc.is_alive()` would still return true.

This can be easily reproduced in linux by running:
1. `huey_consumer.py <test app> -v -k process`
2. `ps -aux | grep huey_consumer` and find the PID for a worker process
3. `kill -9 <pid>`
4. `ps -aux | grep huey_consumer` and notice the zombie process
5. View huey.consumer logs and notice the health check doesn't do anything

Adding a `proc.join()` call with a very small timeout is one way to fix this, there may be others.

items.title: Send SIGTERM after SIGINT
items.body:
Hi again!!!

Usually, when we want to kill a process, we'll first try to gracefully kill it. If it refuses to die, we may send another signal to force it to die.

Currently in `huey`, if we send a `SIGINT` to consumer, it'll set the stop flag and try to join the workers. If the workers refuse to die, the consumer has no choice but to wait. If we send another `SIGTERM` to consumer, it won't work because the corresponding signal handler only sets some variables. There doesn't seem to be a way to tell the consumer to not wait anymore and the second SIGTERM signal may be meaningless.

I think it'll be useful if `huey` provides the option that users can first try to gracefully kill the consumer, and also ungracefully kill the consumer if it won't die.

items.title: Store the real traceback in build_error_result
items.body:
### Problem

A failed task's error result carries a `traceback` field, but it is always the string `'NoneType: None\n'` instead of the real traceback:

```python
from huey import MemoryHuey
from huey.exceptions import TaskException

huey = MemoryHuey(results=True)

@huey.task()
def boom():
    raise ValueError('kapow')

r = boom()
huey.execute(huey.dequeue())
try:
    r.get()
except TaskException as e:
    print(repr(e.metadata['traceback']))   # "'NoneType: None\n'"
```

`error` and `task_id` are correct — only the traceback is lost. Every failed task is affected.

### Cause

`Huey.build_error_result` fills the field with `traceback.format_exc()`:

```python
def build_error_result(self, task, exception):
    tb = traceback.format_exc()
    ...
```

but it is called from `_execute` *after* the `try/except` that handled the task's exception has already completed. In Python 3, `traceback.format_exc()` reflects the currently-handled exception only while inside the `except` block; once control leaves the handler `sys.exc_info()` is cleared, so it returns `'NoneType: None'`. (The `logger.exception(...)` call logs the real traceback because it runs inside the handler — the stored result does not.)

### Fix

Format the exception's own `__traceback__`, which doesn't depend on being inside a handler:

```python
tb = ''.join(traceback.format_exception(
    type(exception), exception, exception.__traceback__))
```

This is the same approach the Django contrib backend already uses (`huey/contrib/djhuey/tasks_backend.py`).

### Tests

Extended `test_api.py::test_task_error` to assert the stored `metadata['traceback']` contains the error class and message. It fails on `master` (`'NoneType: None\n'`) and passes with the fix.

items.title: How to create a dead-letter-queue for tasks that can't be executed?
items.body:
Hey, I've been having fun where sometime we run into a task that's scheduled but which can't be run.

As an example of how this can happen, suppose that you schedule a task to persistent storage but then delete the code that would actually run it and restart the Huey workers.  Now there's a scheduled task that can't run and which will throw an exception when it gets to here.  It'll also stay on the queue, which means the scheduler will keep trying to rerun it. 
https://github.com/coleifer/huey/blob/master/huey/registry.py#L49

(Other ways this could happen include things like a bad custom serializer/deserializer, etc.)

What's the right way to catch errors such as this and make sure that tasks which're in that state don't stay queued?

If it's of any use, I'm happy to send a patch for [api.py:deserialize_task()](https://github.com/coleifer/huey/blob/master/huey/api.py#L299) to add a callback for if a task can't be deserialized?  That way people could decide what to do with it themselves?

items.body:
Saw the following in the docs and having a bit of trouble interpreting it:
> Warning Huey does not guarantee at-least-once delivery of messages, and does not do acknowledgement of completed tasks. This means that if you terminate the consumer without letting it finish any currently-executing tasks, those tasks will be lost. Let's say I send a SIGTERM signal to a consumer, and I have multiple consumers running (in a distributed fashion). Is there a way I can ensure this task will be added back to the queue and retried by another consumer?

items.title: About greenlet worker and OS signals
items.body:
Hi! I'm using the `Greenlet` worker, and noticed that if a signal is received while one of the greenlets is executing (i.e. not "blocked" waiting for I/O), it will be that "thread" the one who handles the signal.

This leads to a somehow troublesome behavior. For instance, when a `SIGINT` is received, it can lead to only one greenlet being stopped, instead of the whole event loop (the other greenlets keep going on).

I just wanted to know your thoughts on this. Is there a way to force that the signal is handled outside the event loop? Should I even worry about this, as the chances of it happening should be extremely low (tasks are heavy on I/O, not CPU)?
